<description>
This is a simple mempool PR that fixes #33510.

Evicting mempool transactions by age (`-mempoolexpiry`, default two weeks) is
incentive-incompatible: it may drop transactions that could still be mined
As discussed IRL and in #33510, this PR hence removes age-based eviction entirely.

Transactions now leave the mempool only via size limiting (`-maxmempool`),
replacement, conflicts, or inclusion in a block. The `EXPIRY` removal reason is
dropped. `-mempoolexpiry` is retained as a hidden no-op that warns when set, so
existing configurations keep starting.

Nice side effects:
- With expiry gone, the `entry_time` index has no readers. Removing it saves an
  ordered-tree node per mempool entry and drops a now unused Boost
  include.
- The `DynamicMemoryUsage()` per-entry estimate drops from three indexes to
  two, so within the same `-maxmempool` budget the mempool fits slightly more
  transactions.
</description>

[2026-10-16] c:6206090292 comment by ajtowns (member):
I don't think it's a good idea to change the node's behaviour in a way that doesn't allow users/miners to revert to the previous default in case the change turns out to be undesirable or harmful for some or many users.

Is there any reason why this change shouldn't be phased in via setting `DEFAULT_MEMPOOL_EXPIRY_HOURS` to a large value, such as 35040 (4 years), instead?
[2026-10-16] c:6216612525 comment by stickies-v (member):
Concept ACK

Node operators should assume that at any point in time, and for any duration of time, their mempool can consume up to `-maxmempool` of resources. Of course, we should make the mempool maximally useful within that constraint, and transactions that should (from the node's perspective) get mined, but don't, can affect its ability to hold transactions that actually will/can get mined.

The main downside from this removal is that in a non-adversarial case (an adversary can just rebroadcast every 2 weeks), transactions can remain in the mempool forever with a high enough fee rate, e.g. in case of diverging policy or consensus rules, and this reduces a node's effective mempool capacity. While that is not ideal, I also don't think we need to have startup options that make it easier to run a node that is out of sync with the policy and consensus rules that the network actually operates on.

I think the other historically mentioned reasons don't hold up anymore either:
- it's nice to be able to replace a large, low fee rate transaction without having to pay the RBF "tax", but RBF mitigates free relay for a reason, I don't think we need a carve-out, even a conservatively rate-limited one
- pinning attacks also seem largely irrelevant, given the 2 week delay and the fact that we have TRUC now
